item.title: Sole Searching: The Science Behind Foot Fetishes
item.description:
Fantasies

Sole Searching: The Science Behind Foot Fetishes

The stats, science, and true stories behind our most fetishized body part.

Posted September 27, 2026

For as long as he could remember, Topher had loved women's feet. From childhood, he noticed his mom's feet when she was barefoot in the kitchen. He spoke of a teacher at school when he was six who wore sandals and flip-flops: "I knew that I felt different, and kind of funny, every time I looked at her feet. I knew I liked them but had no idea why and would often have thoughts about what it would be like to kiss, lick, and tickle them." As Topher began puberty, he started exploring self-pleasure, nearly always to the feet of his hot-toed teachers.

In university, Topher built up the courage to tell his girlfriend about his fetish. Three months into the relationship, he told her, and she took it well, saying that she wasn't surprised, as she'd caught Topher checking out her feet hard.

A very natural question that arises in reaction to the vast world of unique desires is: Why? Are fetishes just quirks of personal experience, or do some have deeper roots—possibly even in our biology?

Although research in this area is scant, there is evidence that some fetishes, like foot fetishes, may have a biological basis. Just as homosexuality is not learned, it is likely that a subgroup of fetishes are simply part of who some of us are. That means that our fetishes can exist independent of our culture, trauma, or formative childhood experiences.

Pop culture has been eroticizing feet for a long time. Ever notice those Quentin Tarantino scenes that are just close-ups of feet, apropos of nothing? Or that time Michael Scott confessed that he'd given up his "one weird thing" in "The Office"—which he suavely hints to be feet—in order to impress a love interest? One could also point to wikiFeet, the celebrity site that allows people to rate, comment on, and obsess over its over 103,560 (and counting!) pics of famous feet.

What Makes Feet So Sexy?

But what is with our obsessive eroticization of feet? One insightful fellow with a foot fetish shared, in response to my question of why, "It's like trying to explain to someone what's so sexy about asses or breasts. You can talk all you want about how soft, round, and cute they are, but if someone doesn't get it on their own, no amount of explaining will change that. The same is true for feet." Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, and when it comes to feet, it seems that either you get it or you don't.

In Justin Lehmiller's studies of fantasies, he found that 14 percent of participants reported having a fantasy about feet at least once in their lives. This study demonstrates the widespread sexual appeal of that most important and useful nether region.

Feet also dominate the fetish community. A study by the International Journal of Impotence Research found that among fetishists, 47 percent of those attracted to body parts focused on feet or toes, while 32 percent of those interested in objects associated with body parts focused on footwear, such as boots or shoes.

Dr. Lehmiller's study of fantasies also found an interesting breakdown of those who had ever engaged in foot play in terms of gender and sexual orientation. He found that 21 percent of gay and bisexual men, 18 percent of heterosexual men, 11 percent of lesbian and bisexual women, and 5 percent of heterosexual women had experienced a foot fantasy. So men are more likely than women to have had a foot fantasy, and queer folks are more likely than straight folks. There is no concrete explanation as to why this is the case, though it is in line with research showing that men are more likely to have fetishes than women.

The Neuroscience of Foot Fetishes

So where does this obsession with feet come from? The most common and compelling explanation for foot fetishes is a neurological one. Our brains process sensations from different parts of the body in an area called the somatosensory cortex, where the feet and genitals happen to be neighbors. Since they sit right beside each other, it makes sense that neural misfirings—when signals between nearby brain regions get crossed or activate together unintentionally—result in cross association rather frequently.

The feet also have an extremely high number of sensory receptors, which means that they're much more sensitive to touch than most other parts of our body, making them more susceptible to pleasure (and pain).

More fascinating evidence for the special relationship between feet and genitals comes from folks who have experienced a foot amputation. Meet Ben, a wonderful man who had his foot amputated six years ago as a result of a horrific car crash. He was open enough to share that although sometimes the area causes him pain, it has also become an erogenous zone. He said:

"I'm a ticklish person in general, and this kind of contact for me does connect with a pleasurable feeling. The interesting thing is, when I massage the stump or run my finger near the scar area, it doesn't tickle or arouse me much. But just as with tickling (you can't tickle yourself), if someone else is doing the massage, or just touching my skin in that area, it's much more intense and pleasurable."

He went on to share that he'd had an embarrassing experience with a physical therapist because he was getting aroused every time she touched that area.

How can neuroscience explain this wonderful piquing of sensuality? We know that when someone loses a leg, especially below the knee, the part of the brain that used to receive signals from the foot suddenly goes quiet. But the brain isn't into wasted space. So over time, the neighboring region of the somatosensory cortex—the part responsible for sensations in the genitals—can start to "spill over" into the area that used to be responsible for sensations in the feet and that is now vacant. This can sometimes lead to a phantom foot becoming sexualized. This results in amputees being able to experience pleasure and even orgasms through the area where their foot once was.

This genital imperialism is known as cortical reorganization—a remarkable example of the ever-evolving nature of the brain and of its penchant for efficiency.

Another wild story showing the relationship between feet and genitals comes from a woman who had foot surgery that led her to experience spontaneous orgasms from inside the incised foot—the first case of foot orgasm syndrome. The woman, known as Mrs. A., had orgasms about five or six times a day, and described feeling them "mainly in the left foot, back under the knee and vagina." Her orgasms were unprovoked, and when doctors stimulated her left foot with an electric current, it sparked an orgasmic response in that very spot!

Doctors hypothesize that the surgery might have led to a confusion of nerve messages, with the brain misinterpreting stimulation of the foot as originating from the vagina. The doctor on the case, Marcel D. Waldinger, hypothesized that "the brain could not anymore differentiate between the foot and the vagina. So that it decided that every stimulus coming from the foot was actually coming from the vagina."

All of this evidence, taken together, really does show that the genitals and feet are neurologically linked. In other words, foot fetishes—like our personalities, our sexual orientations, and what we like to put on toast—are affected by our biological makeup.

Excerpted from Fetish: Smash Taboos and Celebrate What Turns You On.

item.title: Before Sex, There Is Sensuality
item.description:
Sex

Before Sex, There Is Sensuality

Building deeper connection through shared sensory experiences.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Sensuality is the bridge between the friends and the lovers.
  • With young kids, couples try to go from partners straight to lovers. That's a big leap.
  • Sensuality is a great equalizer. It helps partners stuck in parent roles meet at eye level.
Source: Lila Romanelli

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli

Maya and Ben have three young kids and have been stuck in a mommy-son dance for years. This session, Maya mentions they had two good days. I’m curious to hear what changed. "Can you share a specific moment where you felt you were in a different dynamic?"

"We were just sitting on the couch drinking some arak, chatting and laughing," Maya says. The kids kept trying to bother them.

I ask her what Ben did or said that made her feel like they were equals.

"It's just enjoying time without it having to be sex," she says. "Not having to chase."

"So you were just enjoying each other as friends?" I ask. She says yes, and turns to Ben. "Usually the couch is not really a place we hang out together. That's usually where you're half lying down and half working. This time it was different. We playfully sent the kids away. It was just us having fun."

Then I offer them another word. "Between friendship and sexual, there's a category. That's what happened to you on the sofa. That's called sensuality."

I ask each of them to define it. Maya says, "It's the attraction, but without the sex." Ben says, "It's just play. Maybe it goes this way, maybe it doesn't, but that's part of the point. You don't know."

"When you're drinking together, that's a sensual experience," I tell them. "You're sitting on the sofa, your legs are touching, drinking together. This is a perfect example of a sensual, but not a sexual, experience. From there, it could go sexual, or not."

Ben remembers how they first got together: the two of them running around the city discovering restaurants and bars, laughing, eating, and drinking. "The sensual piece was the key," he says. For a moment, they both drift back to sweet memories of a young couple.

Sensuality Is the Highway

Let's play a game. Complete the sentence intuitively:

Sensuality is ________.

For many of us, especially men, sensuality is connected to the world of sex. Yet sensuality is really the experience of all our senses: smell, sight, touch, taste, sound. Sexuality is only one expression of that wider sensory experience. I learned this after 16 years of kissing my wife wrong.

In every marriage, there are three relationships: lovers, partners, and friends. Lovers isn’t just about sex. Lovers meet in eroticism, passion, desire, and romance. Many couples forget that the main arena for lovers is the senses. We knew that in high school, when even standing close or holding hands would send a rush all over our body.

Enjoying time together as equals is also the domain of friendship. When we share simple sensory moments, we're strengthening the friendship too. Sensuality is the bridge between the friends and the lovers.

When you have young children, the partners' bond takes over. Diapers, bedtime, bath time, repeat. Couples lose the everyday sensuality of lovers. Then at night they try to go from partners straight to lovers. That's a big leap, which often leads to rejection and frustration. This is where Maya and Ben kept getting stuck. They couldn't find the bridge back to lovers.

When our kids were born, Galit was touched out. The kids were always hugging and pulling her. She didn't want any more touch. That was hard for me, as my love language is touch. What we didn't know at the time is that sensuality is a wide playground. Touch is just one of the senses.

If couples don't work on their lovers and friends bond during the early child-rearing years, what they're left with is bitter partners. Sensuality is what's going to future-proof your relationship.

The Great Equalizer

Sensuality is a great equalizer. If one of you is holding most of the parental weight, like Maya, it's hard to meet your lover at eye level. After a whole day of being your partner's parent or boss, you don't feel very erotic toward them.

When we both focus on our senses, we move beyond our roles. Two different subjects, feeling something together. It's not a parent and child dynamic anymore. We're both eating ice cream. We’re both enjoying this song. We're rubbing each other's feet. We're both drinking arak.

Sensual Healing

Sensuality lowers the pressure off sex, especially for women. Imagine sexuality as the top of the sensuality pyramid. The wider the base, the higher the peak. Therefore, the best way to improve your sex life is to widen your sensual playground, not just in the bedroom.

Here are a few first steps.

Block out the time. This sounds cheesy, but like anything else, you'll need to put in the reps. Prioritizing sensuality means taking a break from the never-ending logistics.

Decide a priori that it (probably) won't lead to sex. This isn't foreplay. It's a fun exploration of the senses.

Keep it short. Ten minutes. Five minutes. You want to finish with a taste of more. That helps rewire your brain to link your lover with pleasure.

Try different senses. Music, a concert, a sunset, a museum, a meal. Singing together is also sensual. What turns dinner into a sensual experience is your mindset: to connect and enjoy yourself and your partner through the senses. A good place to start is the 30-day touch challenge.

Come as equals. Come as mutual explorers. Get curious about what happens in your body and between you.

Sensuality compounds. You get to experience the song, the meal, the view, through their senses too. I love seeing Galit's reaction to yummy food, as my palate isn't as sophisticated as hers. In those moments, the dish becomes an even richer delight. You get to experience the world twice. Instead of five senses, you get 10. Imagine that.

Now stop imagining. And go get sensual.

Galit Romanelli is a certified relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate in gender studies, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

item.title: What Havana Syndrome May Reveal About the Brain
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

What Havana Syndrome May Reveal About the Brain

The brain may be more vulnerable to some wireless radiation than we thought.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Havana syndrome refers to a cluster of mysterious neurological symptoms reported by U.S. government employees.
  • Some experts believe pulsed microwaves cause the syndrome but the exact mechanism of injury is unknown.
  • Victims' reports hint that cumulative damage from fast-repeating acoustic microtraumas could be responsible.

Havana syndrome, or anomalous health incidents (AHI), refers to symptoms reported by U.S. National Security employees, such as the sudden onset of vertigo, headaches, and loud noises [1]. Many AHI victims report chronic symptoms such as imbalance, headaches, tinnitus, insomnia, and cognitive problems [2]. Neurologists who examined AHI victims describe the cluster of symptoms as being similar to that associated with a concussion or mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) [3].

Both my wife, Dr. Chris Gilbert, M.D., Ph.D., and I have interviewed multiple victims, written articles, and consulted for the U.S. government on AHI. We are also currently conducting laboratory research on the phenomenon using sophisticated RF, thermal, and finite element simulations of the head, brain, and inner ear.

What causes Havana syndrome?

Two expert panels, including those at the National Academy of Sciences and the Intelligence Community, concluded that the most plausible cause of AHI symptoms was pulsed microwaves [4]. Pulsed microwaves are known to produce shockwaves in the brain from rapid local heating that can be heard as clicks, hisses, hums, buzzes, and pure tones. Reports of such sounds by AHI victims are one of the reasons pulsed microwaves have risen to the top of the plausible cause list [5].

Source: Eric Haseltine, with ChatGPT

Implications for brain health

Although the pulsed RF hypothesis of AHI injury has not been proven, if it turns out to be accurate, the implications for the impact of wireless (e.g., microwave) radiation on the brain are profound.

A 2021 study published by the Army Research Lab calculated that concussion-like trauma could be inflicted by a single RF pulse at 1 GHz (Wi-Fi is 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz) with a power density of 10,000 Watts/cm² [6]. That’s an enormous amount of power, but it wouldn’t even be felt as heat if it were delivered in 1-microsecond pulses at a rate of, say, one every ten seconds. With a pulse that short and a repetition rate that low, the average power density at 1 GHz—which is the standard used to limit RF exposure—would be 0.001 Watts/cm², sitting just at the permissible exposure limit [7].

If we increased the pulse rate to one per second and decreased the peak power to 1,000 Watts/cm², that would still stay just at the permissible exposure level for average power. The Army Research Lab scientists who modeled pulsed RF effects on the brain estimated that this power density would produce the equivalent of a collision on the football field [8]. That would equate to ten such collisions in ten seconds at one pulse per second.

Based on those calculations alone, it’s possible that wireless radiation exposure standards, as written, could still allow significant damage from very short pulses.

Data from Havana syndrome victims, however, suggests that much lower peak power densities could be harmful. Two observations support this conclusion. First, many victims report high-pitched tones, which occur during microwave hearing experiments at high pulse rates (>1,000/second) [9]. Second, none of the victims reporting high-pitched sounds described sensations of heat [10], which means that the average power in the exposure—if AHI were caused by RF pulses—would be under the heat detection threshold of 0.065 Watts/cm² average power density.

Assuming 1-microsecond pulses at 1,000 pulses per second, the highest peak power density that would avoid the perception of heat would be about 65 Watts/cm². That is far below the 1,000 Watts/cm² power density equivalent to a football collision. Nevertheless, the acute and chronic symptoms described by AHI victims indicate that 65 Watts/cm², when repeated 1,000 times per second, could be injurious through a previously unknown mechanism of brain injury.

Research on the stretching of neurons in tissue cultures suggests that such a mechanism could be tissue fatigue resulting from repeated brain tissue strain during a rapid series of tissue compressions and expansions, even where individual strains fall below the acute injury threshold [11, 12]. Studies in tissues other than the brain (such as tendons and gums) suggest that cumulative damage from repeated tissue strain cycling—where individual strains are below the injury threshold—is indeed possible [13, 14, 15].

Research on chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in football players further reinforces the notion of brain tissue fatigue because the level of CTE exhibited depends on the total hours of play, not just the number of concussions, implying that many small impacts accumulate into major injury over time [16].

In this regard, it is worth noting that the average wireless power levels permitted in Russia are 0.0001 Watts/cm², a factor of 10 below the U.S. standard [17]. Given that 60 Minutes and others have identified Russian intelligence as the prime suspect in AHI attacks, that is an intriguing difference, to say the least [18].

Perhaps the Russians know something more about how low levels of wireless radiation might harm the brain than we do!

Author’s note on wireless safety

The possibility of harm from wireless exposure at or below power densities allowed by safety standards does not mean everyday exposure to Wi-Fi, cellphones, or other types of consumer wireless radiation is harmful. If AHI was caused by pulsed microwaves, the injury would come from the peak power in each pulse, not the average. A device capable of producing sound inside someone's head fires microsecond bursts whose instantaneous power exceeds a phone's by a factor of millions. Your router and phone have no such peaks—they radiate weakly and irregularly, with nothing resembling that weaponized pulse structure.

item.title: Healing Can Come When You Stop Wanting 3 Things
item.description:
Forgiveness

Healing Can Come When You Stop Wanting 3 Things

People pine for aspects of closure rather than regaining their inner glow.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Attention is your most valuable currency. Remove it from where it isn’t appreciated.
  • Mend the bond you have with yourself by knowing your needs.
  • Never settle for the bare minimum, nor feel you must prove your worth.

“Pain dwells in the invisible thread that keeps pulling you back,” writes Najwa Zebian in The One Who Broke You Can’t Heal You: Let Go of Toxic Bonds and Build Healthy Ones. “Healing requires stepping out of that wounded bond and repairing the bond you have with yourself.”

That’s only one of many gems that Zebian, a Lebanese-Canadian author and educator, extols with her core message that those who break us aren’t the ones who heal us because the wound lives in the bond itself.

When people stop waiting for three things, in relationships especially but also in life, they can find freedom to let go and move on.

1. Stop Waiting for Apologies

When we’re hurt, an apology validates that hurt and begins to make amends. “People who genuinely feel terrible for what they did to you, and who want to fix what they broke, will show you through words and actions,” Zebian writes. They won’t make you question yourself, nor minimize or gaslight your reality. They’ll own it.

What happens, however, when that never occurs? It’s beautiful to get an apology, but do we truly need one? Yes, that acknowledgment can help, but it’s not as if our survival depends upon it.

Don’t ask for that apology. Don’t forgive what might be unforgivable, the author advises. Allow yourself to feel the anger but do not direct it inwardly nor externalize it as if wishing for the wounder to suffer. Instead, remove them from your priority list and build your life outside of them.

2. Stop Waiting for Others to Be What They’re Not

Healthy bonds regulate us, soothe and expand us. If we stay attached or pining for what we may know (but deny) is toxic, we’ll only confuse ourselves and remain stuck. Life contracts rather than expands. And then, most people ponder and ruminate “if only” thoughts, waiting for their person to become who they promised to be and to fix what they broke in the relationship.

Researchers studying expectations for future relationship fulfillment found that people often base their commitment to a relationship more on their expected future satisfaction than with the current level of it, and this affects the pivotal decision of choosing to continue or end it.

Realize that what you had may be over, yet the bond still thrives and that’s why it’s so darn difficult to let go, of all of those unmet needs, the promises made, the dreams planned. Try not to intellectualize it. Walk through the grief of who they were not or didn’t live up to be. For whatever reason, they changed their minds. As the author says, the reason matters not, but the fact is: they changed their minds. You can’t force vulnerability out of someone. Often, it may be nothing about you, and that truth be told, they can’t be honest with themselves. Some endings simply cannot be choreographed.

“Don’t look at yourself as a bad person for seeing someone’s true colors and choosing not to be colored by the same paint brush,” Zebian writes, then later in the book, “Be for yourself what you wish they were for you.”

3. Stop Waiting for Others to Fix You

We find comfort in the familiar, and when we’re at a crossroads (relationships, jobs, other changes), convenience becomes our default. Think about it this way: We cannot invite in another person (job or situation) if we hang on tight, fearing change. With change comes discomfort, hence pushing beyond that zone, which is the focus of so much therapeutic work.

One unique facet Zebian adds to her book is healing threads. An early thread states: “The way out of the darkness is to go through it. The way to a better bond with yourself and with others is through the pain of having to cut the ties that are suffocating you. You free yourself first, then you start over.”

Some mistakes can be repaired, others not so much. Everyone must take on ownership of their problems and work on themselves, knowing when to dig in to do that work and when to turn the page and move ahead. Zebian props up the reader, who often looks to the lost other who might have served that role. The message: You won’t collapse without that person, that place, that job or that situation.

Healthy bonds do steady us. So do healthy jobs and situations. Our sole work is to steady ourselves, and then we more easily find what lifts us up versus what tears us down. We’ll align with common core values, honesty, respect and open, safe communication.

As Zebian wraps up, she says succinctly, “Stop watering the dead plants in your life.” We tend in life to keep trying. How many times have we overwatered plants and pushed them beyond repair? When you’re wilting, water or care for yourself first. Know your limits. Live within them. And thrive.

© 2026 by Loriann Oberlin, MS, LCPC.

item.title: Have School-Based Programs to Improve Sleep Been Successful?
item.description:
Sleep

Have School-Based Programs to Improve Sleep Been Successful?

Some modest gains in student sleep have been attained in school-based programs.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • School-based programs to improve students' sleep have been ongoing for 15 years.
  • Modest gains have been attained in the majority of studies.
  • To achieve better results, programs should have multiple components and extend over a long period.
Source: MoteOo/Pixabay

School-based programs to improve sleep seem to hold promise for reaching large numbers of adolescents, and numerous studies have been reported. As the implications for health problems related to insufficient sleep became apparent beginning in the mid-1990s, survey data showed that the percentage of adolescents getting enough sleep went down. In a 2024 paper, 21 school intervention studies between 2011 and 2022 were reviewed (Gaskin et al. 2024).

Before going into what the review found, let’s look at a typical study. Australian researchers conducted an intervention with a rigorous randomized control group design (Rigney et al. 2015). Using 12 schools, they enlisted 296 students with a mean age of 12.2 years with half assigned to the experimental treatment group and half to a no-treatment control group. The treatment was four weekly classroom lessons followed by a group project on sleep topics, after which the students made a group presentation to their parents. Sleep was assessed both objectively with actigraphy and subjectively through self-report at three time points: before treatment; at six weeks when the program ended, and after 18 weeks. The treatment group had 10 minutes more time in bed than the controls, due to a 10-minutes-later wake time, but the difference was not significant. But at follow-up, even that slight difference between groups was not found. When sleep knowledge and sleep hygiene practices were compared, there were likewise no differences between the groups. The authors concluded that sleep education is important, but more comprehensive, intensive and longer interventions will be required to see good results.

Key Findings From the 2024 Review of School Sleep Interventions

The Gaskin et al. (2024) review included the above plus 20 other school-based studies. Over 10,000 children and adolescents ages 5 to 18 in 13 countries participated. The interventions were primarily classroom sleep education with a few studies adding training in stress management (N=2) and bright light therapy (N=1). Objective and subjective measures of sleep were used as outcomes. The authors found that sleep interventions had minimal to no effect on outcome measures. Moreover, the studies as a group had flaws in study design, measurement, data collection, and analysis. Similar to the conclusions of Rigney et al. (2015), the conclusion was that interventions should have multiple intervention components over a longer time period, and include school administrators, teachers, and parents in addition to students.

In a well-designed study published after the review, Belgian researchers (Vandendriessche et al., 2025) seem to have heeded the suggestions. The intervention took place over 16 weeks—much longer than any interventions that have been done previously. Importantly, students were involved in creating and implementing the various components. Follow-up at six months showed favorable results in knowledge about sleep and barriers to good sleep, better sleep-wake hygiene behaviors (lowered physical activity and less screen use before bedtime), longer sleep, and less sleepiness. At follow-up, the control group’s average sleep was less than at baseline, whereas there was a 12-minute increase in the experimental group. The authors credit student buy-in as a critical aspect of the study, and future studies should aim for replication and extension of these promising results.

item.title: Marvin Minsky, Pioneer of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
Intelligence

Marvin Minsky, Pioneer of Artificial Intelligence

Why Marvin Minsky was way ahead of his time.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Marvin Minsky was a pioneer of artificial intelligence.
  • Minsky foresaw much of how AI would ultimately evolve.
  • Minsky held that thought and emotions were indelibly connected, a radical notion in psychology at the time.

Marvin Minsky of Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Computation Center was one of the founders of the emerging field of artificial intelligence. (Vannevar Bush’s work in computing machines and Norbert Weiner’s in cybernetics had established MIT as a hub of research in the area.) While the term “artificial intelligence” was coined by John McCarthy while at Dartmouth in 1955, Minsky singularly foresaw the future of the technology. “We are on the threshold of an era that will be strongly influenced, and quite possibly dominated by intelligent problem-solving machines,” he stated in 1961, quite accurately describing where we are with AI some 65 years later.

When not thinking literally brainy thoughts (his Princeton Ph.D. dissertation was titled “Theory of Neural-analog Reinforcement Systems and its Application to the Brain-model Problem”), Minsky was able to make the foreign subject of artificial intelligence relatively understandable to a lay audience. “Scientists working on the problem of artificial intelligence are slowly learning how to exploit the structure of the modern computer,” he said, with “magnificent intellectual resources” to be released if the machines could be programmed properly.

Importantly, Minsky drew a distinction between artificial intelligence and existing “thinking machines,” the latter legitimately seen as being able to do only what they were told. Computers were only dull and unimaginative because they had been programmed to carry out tedious tasks by repeating certain designated operations. While very good at following specific instructions, the machines had no ability to solve problems that programmers had not anticipated, which is where artificial intelligence came into the picture.

“We can tell the machine that when specific instructions are lacking it should go ahead by ‘trial and error,’” Minsky explained, a giant leap in the development of the field. With artificial intelligence, “we have traded the task of step-by-step instruction for the harder but more exciting problems of supervising the exploration,” he wrote, defining programmers’ main job as to guide the search process. “The culmination of [these] efforts will come probably within our lifetimes,” Minsky predicted, while admitting that “what will happen then we cannot guess.”

While philosophers were apt to perceive humans as unique beings endowed with moral and ethical qualities that machines could never possess, those with more of a scientific background like Minsky thought otherwise. It was conceivable that computers would not only match humans in all aspects of intelligence but exceed them, he pronounced, an alarming idea at the time.

In 1966, Minsky reported in Scientific American that computers were already setting goals, making plans, generating hypotheses, and identifying relationships—a long way from simply adding or subtracting figures or playing a decent game of checkers. It was not unreasonable to believe that intuition and consciousness were next, he believed, or that people had a monopoly on wit and wisdom.

For Minsky, who was the best-known spokesperson for artificial intelligence in the 1960s, it was the discovery that thought processes could be programmed into computers that made he and others in the field so upbeat about the future of machines. Contrary to popular belief, not every step in solving a problem had to be given to computers, as they were capable of learning from past experiences.

On that basis, it was logical to conclude that the next major breakthrough in artificial intelligence would be what he called analogical reasoning—the ability to recognize similarities between two things, the key to establishing relationships. Human intelligence was currently far ahead on many levels, Minsky conceded, but machines were displaying certain subjective operations of the mind, a sign of much bigger things to come. “It is hard to say how close we are to this threshold,” he said, “but once it is crossed the world will not be the same.”

The creation of a thinking machine had always been the primary objective of artificial intelligence, and it remained so in the 1980s. There was still no consensus on what “thinking” was, however, and theories continued to float about.

Minsky remained very much in the mix, as always offering his take on the subject to both scholarly and popular audiences. In a 1983 article for Psychology Today, Minsky proposed that computers wouldn’t be able to “think” until they could be programmed to have emotions, a rather audacious proposition. Thought and emotions were indelibly connected, he held, and the field of psychology would be well served by bridging the gap between cognitive psychologists, who viewed “thinking” as the key to human behavior, and therapy-based psychologists, who focused on emotions.

This was a radical notion within the psychological community, raising the question of whether such a thing could be possible. Minsky believed it could, although it would take fifty years for the computer equivalent of “emotional knowledge” to be incorporated into programs. (Doing the math, that would be 2033—now not that far away.) Computers could feel something like pride or fear, he suggested, a mechanical interpretation of the human emotion. It might take 200 years for computers to be capable of perceiving the relationship between “themselves” and the external environment, however, something that a typical child could do.

While that remains to be seen, history shows that much of what Minsky had imagined was realized.

item.title: The Gifts We Keep Missing: Rethinking Dyslexia
item.description:
Creativity

The Gifts We Keep Missing: Rethinking Dyslexia

Seeing beyond reading struggles reveals broad strengths and creativity.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Dyslexia affects nearly 1 in 5 people and is rooted in distinct neurobiological brain differences.
  • Dyslexic individuals often show superior 3D spatial visualization and divergent creative reasoning.
  • High verbal reasoning can mask reading struggles in twice-exceptional learners with spiky profiles.

As we enter Dyslexia Awareness Month, the theme "The Gifts We Keep Missing" feels more relevant than ever. This October, I am speaking at the American Academy of Pediatrics National Conference in San Diego about the critical role pediatricians and primary care providers play in recognizing and supporting dyslexic children. Affecting approximately 17% of the population—nearly 1 in 5 individuals—dyslexia is highly common, neurobiologically based, and highly heritable. Yet, it is frequently misunderstood and missed, especially when we only look for what is going wrong.

Dyslexia often follows a late-blooming course, much like a lotus flower. In a child's early years, reading and spelling challenges can obscure their innate talents. However, with appropriate, evidence-based educational supports, those early difficulties can become manageable, allowing the child's true strengths to flourish and grow stronger over time.

Modern research consistently shows that the dyslexic brain brings remarkable, measurable advantages. These neurobiological findings are strongly reflected in community data; in a survey of over 1,000 dyslexic adults conducted by Dyslexic Advantage, the vast majority reported specialized strengths in these areas:

  • Superior 3D Spatial Reasoning: Research studies have documented the superior abilities of dyslexic individuals on tests of mental rotation and spatial paper-folding tasks. As legendary ocean explorer Dr. Robert Ballard explains in The Dyslexic Advantage movie, his capacity for vivid mental simulation allowed him to visualize the ocean floor in 3D, replaying various possible scenarios in his mind that ultimately allowed him to discover the wreck of the Titanic where others had failed.
  • Divergent Creativity: Recent meta-analyses reveal that adults with dyslexia show significantly greater divergent creativity, scoring higher on alternative uses and creative insight tasks compared to non-dyslexic peers.
  • Connecting Ideas: Dyslexic individuals often show stronger performance when forming unusual combinations of ideas and have superior recognition memory.

Unfortunately, a deficit-only view of dyslexia remains prevalent. This outdated perspective is inaccurate and places a heavy emotional burden on children and their families, often resulting in students being told to lower their expectations. This toll is especially severe for twice-exceptional (2e) students—children who are gifted but also have significant dyslexia-related challenges.

Comprehensive cognitive testing of these students often reveals "spiky profiles," characterized by exceptionally high verbal comprehension but highly discrepant, low oral reading fluency and working memory. When these children have the conceptual reasoning of a sixth grader but the reading and spelling skills of a second grader, the disconnect can lead to intense shame, anxiety, and withdrawal.

Furthermore, dyslexia is frequently masked by co-occurring conditions. ADHD and reading disabilities co-occur in 25% to 40% of cases. It is crucial to recognize that medically treating a child's ADHD will not address the core reading issues of their dyslexia; specific, structured literacy instruction is required.

As MIT Professor and MacArthur Fellow Dr. Catherine Drennan has shared, the unique way the dyslexic brain visualizes shapes and patterns can be a massive advantage in solving complex scientific problems that leave others stuck. By fostering a balanced, strengths-based understanding of dyslexia, we can replace stigma with self-esteem, resilience, and true school engagement for these remarkable learners.
